utterances.text: These sound to me like guide-lines on how to do it rather than a plan for particular activities that you know you are going to undertake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These sound like general guide-lines. They do not sound like a specific plan for a specific activity such as a search. Now, am I misunderstanding the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you're right, Your Honour. That is part of what a plan should contain for an activity that is carried out by the members of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cepic, if you have a particular point to make about something that happened in Kosovska Mitrovica that's inconsistent with the plan or has something to do about the plan, you better make it quickly because your cross-examination must now come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm almost at the end, Your Honour. Just a couple of questions in relation to the planning from the secretariat of internal affairs. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bogunovic, very simply, the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica is supposed to carry out a blockade and search, they are trying to capture some terrorists, four or five terrorists in the area of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, who assesses the situation and who makes the plan?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, in order to do anything there has to be information about that. After information is received, then people who a competent for this meet, members of the OKP, the police, and the immediate superior, and that is the chief of SUP, or rather, an officer authorised by him. A plan of activity is made, and after that the dangerous perpetrators of the crime are captured, either terrorists or persons who are drug pushers or whatever else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Who specifically draws up this plan?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The authorised official, authorised by the chief of the secretariat, and in this kind of a situation it would be the head of the police department together with the chief of the OKP. And all persons who took part in drawing up this plan would sign this plan, meaning that they had drawn up the plan, plan approved by, and I agree. That is what the last page would look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Bogunovic, I have that kind of a plan from the SUP of Pec and that is what the last page looks like.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: These are regular documents that we -- well, not to say every day, but certainly once a week we have such documents created.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just one more document at the end. You mentioned the concept of a Joint Command existing in 1981. Let me just ask you one question with regard to that and then we'll be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up P1508.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, can you see this document from 1993 before you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it is not the Joint Command in the sense of "zdruzena komanda, zdruzena komanda," those were members from all the republics of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How is this going to help us, Mr. Cepic, to analyse the situation in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With your leave if we see the third page they mention Joint Command in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what? No, please remove it. That's the end of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have to prioritize what you're doing and give us material that directly impinges on the real issues in the case. We're not hear to explore the history of the use of the expression Joint Command in the former Yugoslavia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you were appointed to the -- to be deputy chief of SUP Kosovska Mitrovica, did you receive a written letter of appointment?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I received a decision on my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not a person who collects decisions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- pertaining to him. There were quite a few of them and it all exists in my dossier or file.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who gave you that decision?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was handed over to me by my chief of secretariat, Ljubinko Cvetic. The decision was signed by Vlastimir Djordjevic, chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So that is when you arrived in Kosovska Mitrovica in November 1998 that Mr. Cvetic handed over to you a decision?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who told you to go down to Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: My superior, Colonel Adamovic, chief of the secretariat of the Djakovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you discuss your appointment to Kosovska Mitrovica in November 1998 with anybody in the MUP staff for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Cvetic in November and you say that he handed over to you a document, did he tell you who it was who told him that you were to be appointed as a deputy in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who had told him. I told you who sent me to Kosovska Mitrovica, so I really can't say. The man was here, perhaps you should have addressed that question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, unhappily it wasn't brought to our attention that you would say what you have when he was here, but I suggest to you that he did not give you any writing about your appointment.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know on the basis of what you are claiming that since you were not there. I was there and I signed that in the presence of my chief of secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm under oath, I can only tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you at any time -- well, I suggest to you also that it was Mr. Lukic, General Lukic, and Mr. Mijatovic who told him that you were to be appointed to -- as a deputy in Kosovska Mitrovica. Do you know of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. This is too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We want -- if he is suggesting, we want the source. Where is the source for this claim?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Quotation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, counsel can help you if he wishes, but he doesn't need to disclose a source for putting the question. All that matters is the answer. The question is immaterial unless the witness accepts it and answers it. But if he wishes to assist you, then he will. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As you know, Mr. Cvetic was here and these questions were not asked of him, but since we have received this statement we have had to get instructions from Mr. Cvetic in respect to what this witness is now alleging. And I put the question to him on the basis of those instructions. In any case, as indicated by the Court, I don't think I need to tell him that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If this is represented as Mr. Cvetic's testimony, we want him back to cross him on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not being represented as his testimony. You misunderstand the situation. It's the source of a question. And what becomes testimony depends on the answer. This is a real problem in this case because the Defence have failed constantly to put to witnesses points that will turn out to be controversial when the Defence witnesses come here; and therefore the Prosecution are put in the invidious position of having to go back to witnesses to check up and see if what's being said by a subsequent witness is true or not because it was never put and never challenged at the time of the original witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was nothing to be challenged on this matter at that time. Cvetic never testified about it. Why should I challenge something he never testified about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you know that you're going to lead evidence about the point, don't you think it's fair to give the person who's going to be criticised an opportunity to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How am I going to know two years ago? What should I have done? At that time I have never met Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is one of the problems of this case, that the preparations aren't done at the right time, but that's something we're going to have to cope with as we go along. But there's nothing improper about further investigations in these circumstances being carried out by the Prosecution and the Prosecution putting the results of these investigations to witnesses for witnesses to comment. That's perfectly proper. So that objection is repelled. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you went to Kosovska Mitrovica in November 1998, did Mr. Cvetic not indicate to you that it was General Lukic and Mr. Mijatovic who had directed him that you were coming there to assist?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who told Mr. Cvetic to hand in the decision. I was already in Kosovska Mitrovica when my decision arrived, that is to say that I had spent several days in Kosovska Mitrovica without the decision. And then following that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it that your answer is that you did not hear from Mr. Cvetic that it was Mr. Mijatovic and General Lukic who told him that you were going to be assigned there as his deputy?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I truly wasn't present and nobody told me who had told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were there there was another deputy, deputy chief of the SUP for Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You went there and joined him?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were responsible for police activities or police matters and duties in the field or to assist in that regard?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in accordance with the regulations in force at the time and in accordance with the job description of the deputy chief of Kosovska Mitrovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I may -- I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you told that you were there to assist in respect to police activities out in the field, that was your responsibility, prime responsibility, as deputy chief of the SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities when you went there? What were you told that you were supposed to be doing down there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: My duty was to stand in for the chief of the secretariat when he wasn't there and to work in accordance with instructions and tasks issued to me by him. If necessary, I can enumerate everything written in the documents and regulations that can be found in the ministry, but this is in brief what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you involved in -- okay. Very well. You said that General Stevanovic visited the SUP on one occasion and he told you to accompany him out to the field where there was some action going on. I think that's at paragraph 67 of your statement, that's anti-terrorist action at Bajgora at the end of April, beginning of May. What was your role when you accompanied General Stevanovic out there into the field? In other words, what did he ask you to go with him to do?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I received this order from my superior to go and accompany General Obrad Stevanovic to the location where there was a joint activity of the police and the army. As far as I was told, there was information that in the Bara and Bajgora area there was a stronghold, a hospital, and headquarters, and General Obrad wanted to go there to the location and I accompanied him. General Obrad met up with the members of the Ministry of the Interior there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- the personnel that was involved in that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just wanted to know what was your role, do you know what General Obradovic [sic] expected of you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: There is no General Obradovic, but General Obrad Stevanovic wanted me to take him safely there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: To take him safely to the location where he wanted to go, given that he was not familiar with the area --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you were escorting --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I was somebody who had spent quite some time in the area at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you were acting as the escort of General Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It is a custom to have one of the officers of the Ministry of the Interior meet or welcome high officials of the MUP and to remain with them for as long as they stay in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, was this the first or the only time that you escorted General Stevanovic around?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That was not the first time, but it was the first and only time in the territory of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, if we could return to the earlier part of your statement you said, I think, in paragraph 5 of your statement that there's no need for the -- as far as you knew, for the SUPs to get the permission or the agreement of the MUP staff to carry out tasks. Weren't there -- or without showing you a document are you willing to allow that there were some extraordinary tasks where the plans of the SUPs would have to be submitted to the MUP staff in Pristina for approval?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that a document was sent to the MUP staff because we didn't draw up any plans, or rather, we draw up plans, nothing else. A secretariat draws up a plan of activities for certain activities that need to be done. I explained that when Mr. Cepic put questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you not have to submit plans for anti-terrorist action to the MUP staff of Kosovo for approval? Now, you might not know. If you don't know, say you don't know, you were deputy chief.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know whether that was our duty; and if it was, then the chief of secretariat knew about that because I worked exclusively on the basis of his instructions. I wasn't the decision-maker. I was somebody who made suggestions. Now, whether my suggestions would be accepted or not, that was up to the person above me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you would not be aware that at various meetings at the MUP staff both General Stevanovic and General Lukic instructed the chiefs of the SUPs and the various PJP detachments that they should submit plans to the MUP staff for Kosovo for approval?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we need to distinguish between activities aimed at terrorism and regular activities within the secretariat where I served. When it comes to regular activities within the ministry, we had no duty to provide any plans except in our own specialty departments. As for the plans and activities carried out by PJPs, I can't say anything about that because I was not a member of a PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. So therefore that section of your statement at paragraph 5, when you said there was no need or obligation of the chief of the secretariat and his subordinates to have the agreement and permission of the MUP Pristina prior to carrying out their duties, you're talking about the regular duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. As for the rest, I can't say anything because I wasn't a participant. I can speculate and I can give some arbitrary answers --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- which is not in the -- which is not going to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Also at paragraphs 4 and 79 you speak about reporting to the MUP staff. At one stage you said that you were required to report to the MUP staff in paragraph 4 but then you said that during the war it was impossible to communicate with the staff in paragraph 79. Well, let us look at the last sentence of paragraph 79. Are you saying in this sentence that it was impossible to communicate with the staff by a mobile telephone but it was possible to communicate otherwise?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: When it comes to mobile phones, at that time we had no mobile phones and everything else had been destroyed by NATO. So there was no communication either with the MUP or with any other institution within the Ministry of the Interior. We only had radio stations and those worked under -- with great difficulty, since there was no electricity and we couldn't charge batteries in order to use them and also due to a very limited range of these radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So -- but you could communicate with other agencies and units of the MUP as well as the MUP staff Pristina by courier and by special telephone lines, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Special telephones were also connected to the regular telephone lines of PTT. As for the other services of the ministry which were in the territory of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, we had only courier contact with them. We know that the SUP building was hit and that all units were dislocated throughout the entire town of Kosovska Mitrovica. The conditions were extremely difficult. We had numerous problems in work and coordination. All of us officers in all units had problems. When I say "units," I mean organizational units, you have to bear in mind that I have military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the bombing how did you communicate with the MUP staff in Pristina? How were the reports sent?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not send any reports to the MUP staff either during the bombing, before the bombing, or after the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. How were the reports sent to the MUP staff during the war? Whether or not you sent them, do you know how they were sent?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: When necessary, given that we were duty-bound to send information to the MUP staff in Belgrade, and as for the staff in Pristina, that was covered by couriers exclusively, as far as I know. I am not a signals person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you would not know if special telephone lines were set up after the PTT building was bombed, would you?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Had there been such lines, I think I would have known about it because after all, I was person number two within the secretariat. They attempted to fix something, but that was very difficult, and even if it existed it lasted only for a short period of time because the relay in the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica was bombed on a daily basis, the repeater, and generally they were bombed frequently, all repeaters were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware of orders from General Lukic to the chiefs of the SUPs and to the head of the detachments that they were obliged to report all security-related incidents to the staff? And this is during the bombing.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: This information never reached me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you were in your office every day, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how often were you in the office during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the war we did not have offices --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- given that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every six to seven days we changed the location of the chief of the secretariat, and I was there next to him or in a place where he ordered me to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you were always with him throughout the war, more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wouldn't say next to him, but we would meet up in the morning and he would tell me, Today you will go and tour Zubin Potok or Leposavic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I wish if you're not going to say something, you wouldn't say it. I'm only quoting back your own words to you. Anyway, you tell us you had no idea that these SUPs were supposed to report to the MUP staff, that's your position, you had no idea about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when it comes to reporting, I wrote in my statement and I also said how the staff in Pristina was informed and about what matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just answer my question, please. You had no idea that the SUP was supposed to report to the MUP staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again the MUP staff is something that exists in Belgrade, the so-called operations centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm referring -- I'm sorry if I haven't made it clear, I'm referring to the MUP staff in Pristina. You're saying you had no idea that the SUP was supposed to report to the MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We obviously have not understood each other. The MUP staff was informed, the one in Belgrade, and then information only or on an only-information basis, that was the duty with respect to the MUP staff in Pristina. That's what I wrote, and the Prosecutor asked me how we sent the reports and I explained to him that there were no telephone lines and that I was not a signals person and I didn't know how this was sent. As far as I know, every report that was sent either to Belgrade or to Pristina, to the staff there, during the bombing was sent via a courier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't want to -- I'm not interested in that part of the matter. I'm interested in what your obligations were, and you should have understood that from the questions. Now tell me, what was the point of the MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can't speak about something that is not within my competence. The MUP staff did not fall under Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, that was a body that was above me so I can't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this time am I right in thinking you can't think of any reason why there was a MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have P1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Here we have the minutes of a meeting at the MUP staff on the 14th of April, 1999, that's Pristina MUP staff. You can see from the first page that present was General Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what's the point in asking a witness who knows absolutely nothing about the MUP staff about the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask him about the MUP staff directly, I was going to ask him about what I was asking him about before, the obligation to report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do we need this document? He's told you what the obligation to report was. As far as he's concerned he didn't know what any obligations were and he told you that they reported some information and that's all they did. What more do you need to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness I think has gone further than that and is suggesting that there was no obligation as far as he knew to report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, he didn't know of an obligation is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he also said as deputy chief he would know about circumstances surrounding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, what more do you need? This is a man who doesn't know he's supposed to report, we've got that much, but he did report from time to time. What more do you need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let me ask a specific question without showing the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that General Lukic specifically commanded all of these people you see here as present at this meeting except General Obradovic [sic], who was a superior, to report all security-related events to him? Do you know that? General Obrad Stevanovic, I meant. Thank you very much, counsel. Did Mr. Cvetic tell you that General Lukic ordered them to report security-related matters to him and the staff; if so, your answer is yes, if not it is no.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that Colonel Adamovic made me aware of that while I was in Djakovica, yes, that I should inform the MUP in Belgrade and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Pristina...

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- CC the MUP in Pristina. That's what I said just now, that is to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- that when I arrived and when I was given the assignment of reporting at the Djakovica SUP the then-chief of secretariat told me what my duties and responsibilities were there, and he said to me that all information pertaining to what happened in the territory of the secretariat, as done in my home secretariat, should go to the DOC and that we should also, by way of information, send this to the Pristina staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And apart from that, reporting, copying the Pristina staff, you know of no other reporting to the Pristina staff; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously you and I are not understanding each other. There is daily information, periodical information, monthly information, biannual information, periodical information going to the MUP, that is what I CC'd the staff in Pristina on. All other reports that we compiled within the secretariats were sent only along the lines of work. We were not duty-bound to send those reports to the MUP staff in Pristina in -- by way of information or in any other way. If you have other questions I may clarify, but it seems that we understand each other now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll just take your answer that you don't know. Can we discuss briefly issue of the reserve police officers. When the reserve police squads were being formed, did General Lukic and the MUP staff issue a plan or plans in respect to their organization?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was not in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. I arrived on the 20th of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- in the area of the Djakovica SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When they were being formed, wherever you were, did General Lukic not issue plans in respect to their organization?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: My first encounter with reserve police squads was in the Djakovica SUP, and that is what my chief told me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, if you know if General Lukic issued plans in respect to the organization of these reserve police squads, just tell me yes; if you do not, say no. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know of General Lukic issuing such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we need to find a place to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps we could do so now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How much longer do you envisage being?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think perhaps I could take the rest of the session -- of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We won't allow you to do that, I'm afraid. You normally get an hour with a witness like this, who's presented on a 92 ter basis and you haven't suggested any reason why we should extend that. You've had about 40 minutes so perhaps you would make a point of completing within half an hour. We'll resume at 6.00. Mr. Bogunovic, we have to have a break at this stage for half an hour. Please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was my understanding that you have one hour of cross-examination with a witness who has given a 26-page 92 bis statement. I just want to know the Rules because I came here with a different understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My understanding is that the time spent with a witness with so much information was certainly in excess of one hour, I can't give you a precise time, but I did not know there is a one-hour limit. If there is, I am prepared to comply with it because it is the responsibility of the Court to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's a guide-line that has been in operation since the case began.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One hour for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where it's a 92 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- witness presented on that basis. We've always said that if good reason was shown we would extend these periods. But so far this cross-examination has been virtually unproductive and doesn't on the face of it appear to be worth pursuing unless you can start focussing on issues that really are going to increase our knowledge of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if you do that and you create interest and demonstrate that there are issues that require to be explored the position may be different, but that's not the message that's coming over so far. Anyway, we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, perhaps before we close the issue I wish to address the issue when we resume because there are issues which I wish to cover in the half-hour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've wasted an awful lot of time on stuff that's really been --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that's a matter of your judgement, but perhaps if that could be indicated at some point in the course of when I'm asking the questions, then I could address you on it and I could tell you exactly where I'm going. Anyway, I don't want to get involved in any argument about this. I should just express that I am surprised; however, I will abide by the ruling in respect to the one hour, but I'm surprised about one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the order which was made in relation to the use of time in October 2006 what we said was that: "For witnesses whose evidence primarily and in accordance with the practice of the Prosecution followed in the trial so far is brought pursuant to Rule 92 ter, the Prosecution shall have a maximum of 30 minutes to conduct both direct and re-examination. The Defence collectively shall have a maximum of 60 minutes for cross-examination of such witnesses. The Defence shall consult among themselves to decide on the apportionment of time," and when we established the regime for the Defence case we said that would apply mutatis mutandis; if it did, you wouldn't even have 60 minutes. It's through our interpretation that it's only right the Prosecution should have that 60-minute time that that has been the practice we've followed so far without enforcing it rigidly. But I'm surprised that you're not aware of that rule, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'll have to refresh myself. Clearly, I had forgotten. If it's one hour, it's one hour, as I indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless there are good reasons for it being longer, and we shall see if that situation develops. We shall now resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that General Lukic issued orders for the organization of the RPOs in 1998?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that the RPO squad were available for use in plans made by the MUP staff Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware that the RPOs, the reserve police squads, were available for use in plans that were issued by the MUP staff Pristina?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "use." I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For deployment -- okay. You don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can respond, if I may, why the RPO were established, if that is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You have already done that in your statement, sir. I have not asked you that. Now, General -- sorry, not general, Mr. Cvetic told us that the RPOs existed during the war while he was in Kosovska Mitrovica and they participated in expelling people from their homes. You are saying that all of them were disbanded. I would like us to look at P1996, and I will ask you a couple of questions about that. P1996 is a minute of the MUP staff meeting for the 7th of May, 1999. Do you have it there? If we could scroll down on the B/C/S copy a little bit. Can you see at number, well, you don't need to scroll down, at number 5 that you were present as deputy chief for the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I never attended a single meeting of the staff in Pristina except for when I was promoted on the fast track, and I came towards the end of the meeting when I was handed over a decision on appointment -- on an extraordinary appointment to a higher rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, that is not precisely what I was asking you, but I think I need to explore that answer a little bit. When did you attend this meeting of the MUP staff in Pristina where you were promoted, when, that is date or approximate date?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am of the view that this is the date when I was present but only at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mean the 7th of May?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, who handed over to you this decision on your appointment to a higher rank at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Obrad Stevanovic, General Obrad Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What rank was that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was promoted from lieutenant-colonel to lieutenant-colonel. It sounds a bit funny but that's the way it was. The reason was the following: While I was in Kosovo and Metohija I had the rank of major. My superiors who sent a proposal for my extraordinary promotion did not know that I already had that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, so you were --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: And a rank is obtained on the basis of a particular job. You could not get a higher rank unless you have a job providing for that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you were officially promoted to lieutenant-colonel at that time. Was it normal for persons to receive documents in respect to their promotion and appointments at MUP staff Pristina meetings?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As for extraordinary promotions, in the Ministry of the Interior this was the first time that someone received an extraordinary promotion. It was the three of us from the ministry that were promoted. That was the first time as far as I know in the ministry that someone received this fast track promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know why it was done at a MUP staff Pristina meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: My assumption is that it was done because of the presence of high officers from the Ministry of the Interior, that is to say the assistant minister, Obrad Stevanovic, and the chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were the other two persons who received this fast track promotion present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, all three of us were down there at the restaurant, in a restaurant, and after that we were invited to come in at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was your only role you played in that meeting, to receive your promotion?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: My only role at the staff meeting and my presence at any MUP staff in Pristina was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Let me get back to what I was asking you about. You will see here at page 5 of the English at the bottom and page -- the top of page 5 of the B/C/S that you gave a report at this meeting including very detailed figures as to what was happening in your territory. Don't you recall doing that, giving quite an elaborate report including precise numbers as to what was happening in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said to you that at this meeting I never spoke, neither did I speak at any meetings at the staff. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So therefore --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- and I don't know who kept minutes, but I think that since the chiefs of SUPs were placed, the person who kept the minutes didn't know the name of the chief of the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP and seeing me there he put my name into the minutes. As for the situation in the territory of Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, I can give a comment concerning each item individually because I attended meetings held by the chief of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not asking you about that. You are saying as explanation that the person didn't know the name of the chief, so seeing you there, he puts your name, but he describes it you look at it, deputy chief. You don't recall making those representations at the meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was only on that day that I received my promotion. I'm under oath here and I state with full responsibility that I never spoke at any staff meetings, I never uttered anything, I never took the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Looking at what's recorded under your name, can you confirm to us that the information recorded is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I haven't read this, could this be zoomed in so that I can look at it and then tell you. This information here is familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As to the figures, I can't say they are fully correct, but in general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The other persons mentioned there as chiefs of SUPs in Kosovo - if we could go back to the front page - did you know these people, Colonel Bogoljub Janicevic, Colonel Vlahovic, Milan Stanojevic, Milos Vojinovic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Some yes, some no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing them at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I came to that meeting where I was handed in the decision on my promotion with my chief. I know some of the people, some I don't know. I spoke to some of the people before the meeting and most of them congratulated me on my extraordinary promotion, they did that after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Remind us who your chief was at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vucina Janicijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you hear the reports and the instructions that were issued at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: On the following day, yes, from my chief of the SUP because it is customary, or rather, it is a practice to have the chief come to a meeting and inform his associates about the tasks that need to be performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, your chief is not recorded as being present there. There is a Janicevic, but that was Bogoljub from Pristina. Your chief was not at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I've already said once that I attended the meeting at the very end when the decision on my promotion was given me. My chief, Vucina Janicijevic, was present at the meeting and he presented the information that you asked me about and I said that I know about that and I can comment on that. But I myself did not make any representations. Had I done that I see no reason why I wouldn't have mentioned that here. Why would I comment on the information presented by my chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... answering my question directly. If we could look at the last page of that document, please, 1996, you will see - and the last page of the English as well, please - you will see that General Lukic in closing the meeting said: "Members of the RPOs may not wear police uniforms and this must be prohibited immediately." Now, this indicates that RPOs existed at that time and that General Lukic was aware of their existence. Did you hear that said by General Lukic or did your superior tell you about that instruction in respect to the RPOs?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that at the meeting because after the meeting was over we who had been promoted on an extraordinary basis at the meeting held in Kosovska Mitrovica, the chief, Vucina Janicijevic, told us that we needed to check whether there was a single RPO that hadn't been disbanded and whether there was a single uniform -- member wearing a uniform in the populated area since we had already been conveyed this information about the RPOs being disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you are now saying that you were told to check. So when you checked were there -- well, did you find any RPOs in Kosovska Mitrovica SUP area?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not the person who could check all of that. At the meeting chaired by the chief of the secretariat there were people in attendance who had the area under their control. They provided information, and as far as I know it was said that there was not a single RPO out there except for some individual cases where a citizen may have kept a part of the uniform that had been out of use by the Ministry of the Interior. When I say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- "out of use," that means that it wasn't a valid uniform anymore because uniforms had changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we could move on. You went in late April/early May with General Stevanovic to the area where the Bajgora operation was being conducted and you saw -- later on in the day you saw a convoy. Where was it -- when I say a convoy I mean a troop, a group of refugees. Where was it you saw these refugees first?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In my statement I said that I had been ordered to go to the town of Vucitrn, which is an OUP within the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP, because there was a large group of people there who had left --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just tell me where, that's a place, name the place on the road where you saw this group of refugees.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I was about to tell you. It's an intersection of roads, Vucitrn-Pristina and Samodreza-Pristina -- no, I apologise, Vucitrn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many refugees?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Many.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you approximate?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Since I'm a person who provided security at many sports matches, I would give you an estimate of 15 to 20.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, there were members of the OUP, the O-U-P, Vucitrn that accompanied them to the agricultural complex or persuaded them to go to the agricultural complex. How were these members of the Vucitrn OUP attired?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the Vucitrn OUP wore a regular blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean in paragraph 68 where you say you were the only one who wore a blue uniform?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 68 pertains to my stay in Bajgora with the members of a PJP. If you read it carefully you'll see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you said you were ordered to reconnoitre and report on this convoy. Who ordered you to do so?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of the secretariat, Vucina Janicijevic, who was the only one authorised to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And how long did you remain with this convoy?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I started telling you about that and you interrupted me. I spent about one hour with the refugees convincing them that they were safe --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just asked you how long now. You spent one hour with the refugees in all?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you go to the -- the correctional facility, this Smrekovnica correctional facility that day?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Not on that day, and I never went to Smrekovnica, to the prison there, but on that day I passed by it because I went back to the SUP, that is to say to the location where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, you said that one of the reasons why you said that people were mistreated or killed at that facility was because there was a register of the persons who were arrested there. Do you know where that register is or where that was kept?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would object at this point, Your Honour, because it appears to my learned friend is suggesting that the witness said that people were mistreated and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if that was the case perhaps I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is this, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is line 13, clearly I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are saying, sir, that there is a register of the persons who were kept at the facility, and that is one of the reasons why you say people were not mistreated and killed in the facility. Do you know where the register is kept?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I work for the Ministry of the Interior. The prison belongs to a different ministry, to the Ministry of Justice, I'm not sure exactly what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: So that's who you need to direct your question at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So does your answer mean that you don't know where it's kept? You can say I don't know, you know, you don't need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness answered the question, it's not recorded, but the witness said: You should address Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's not an ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But your police officers -- I take it you mean you don't know where it is kept. Your police officers or police officers from your SUP were allowed to enter that correctional facility to interrogate prisoners, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the OKP asked for approval from the court in order to be able to talk to them. A patrol as we call them in the police was sent consisting of members of the O KP and crime technicians with the prior approval, and that was the only way for them to enter the premises of the prison, not just this prison, any other prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, where is the reference to this register?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it was used, the word "register" was used as a word but in a context that indicates that there was a register. It's in paragraph 87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, 87, I'm at 67, sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know -- to move on, did you know Agim Hajrizi personally? You spoke about him in paragraph 88 of your statement. Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I never communicated with the gentleman, but he was mentioned quite often. His name was often mentioned at meetings that I attended, these meetings that were chaired by the chief of SUP or somebody else, and I always had -- I always heard good things about that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You are saying that he was an opponent of the KLA. That view is not based on your personal association with him?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know a police -- time is limited --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know a policeman in your SUP called Nenad Pavicevic, P-a-v-i-c, with a full diacritic, e-v-i-c with a half diacritic, Pavicevic.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: SUP Mitrovica had about 2.000 policemen, so I cannot remember that name, but if there is a particular incident involved perhaps you could remind me and then I'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that he was convicted by the interim court set up by the UN in Kosovo in 2000 in absentia for the murder of Mr. Hajrizi, one of your -- one of the police officers associated with your SUP? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I spent only seven, or rather, eight months in the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP after I left --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You also made various references to 101 references, it is noted here, to 6D614, that's a document I think you were shown by the Defence. Maybe I should refer you to where you have done it in your statement. Maybe have a look at paragraph [sic] 57 of your statement and the succeeding paragraph. You make various references to this document. But before I ask you about these documents, at one of the references, 6D614, page 57, item 84, that you made it is stated here that in respect to the killing on Lazar Street of Agim Hajrizi, the bodies were identified as Agim Hajrizi, his wife Nazmija Hajrizi, and their child Iljir Hajrizi. Were these the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was not on the actual spot. The operatives from the criminal police and the crime technicians were there. There's no reason for me not to trust them because a record was compiled on the basis of which the corpses were identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you about the record from 6D614 which you have made many -- 101 references to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph is this in? I can't find it in paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's 6D614, page 57 in the English, paragraph 84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say that's in paragraph 57 of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, this is in paragraph -- referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's what we have so far --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 88 of statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, you referred to a document in your statement and the document is before you now, and you see at item 84 and I think the wrong --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wrong -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not an employee of Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me. The -- this is not the corresponding item 84.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need page 57, paragraph 84. There's one -- the English is Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The English is correct, but this is not the -- and I think now we have the correct B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I just want --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, you can tell me after we've finished the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back it. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you read the first paragraph of this item 84, please.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: "On the 24th/25th of March, 1999, Skenderi Plana (civilian) reported that in Tsar Lazar Street number 7 there are three corpses identified as those of Hajrizi Agim, his wife, Hajrizi Nazmija, and their child Hajrizi Iljir who had been killed" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What the witness read, it's not what the witness read. It's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask the translator to translate on the basis of what he said and not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That is exactly what we did on the basis of what he was reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your complaint, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 4 of the text says mother, not wife, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can the interpreter assist us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: His mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the interpretation was correct, the witness was wrong, that's been established. It should be mother. Let's continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you -- you said that you weren't involved in that particular investigation. Did you write any official reports in respect to these items that you have referred to from 6D614, from this document that you were shown?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see in this case the investigating judge was in charge of the proceedings --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, stop --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: -- and, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have to stop you there. You said enough about this case. I'm just asking you, in respect to all of these references that you make to this document that you were shown by the attorneys for Mr. Lukic, did you write any reports for any of them that you referred to, any official reports? Were you personally involved in these investigations?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not an investigating organ and there is no need for me to write up anything concerning the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That means no, you weren't involved in these investigations?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I was not involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I always say that for that there is a field of work that is covered by certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So basically --

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I conduct analyses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So when you refer to 6D614 or sections from it in your statement, is that simply because you've read them? That's the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. My source is the fact that I was on the spot, in Kosovska Mitrovica I mean, where my subordinates wrote reports about the incidents that occurred on different days, and on the basis of that I included that in my statement because I remember about these incidents and I know. But in most cases I was not present, I was not on the spot because had I gone to all the scenes I would be -- I would have been a person who was only involved in on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, please listen to the questions and just answer what you're asked. Does that mean that you know about these incidents through reading the reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, now are you about finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, in paragraph 96 of this statement there is reference to an exhibit 3D181, which I notice is produced in e-court as a whole book although you're relying on only one page of that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we need only that one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, would you please scan the page and the cover page of the book and substitute them for the whole book and withdraw the book, and meanwhile that exhibit will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bogunovic, what is your current employment?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I am now employed in PP Zlatica AD Lazarevo, which is an agricultural company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, why did you leave the police?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Does that matter to this Court? If necessary, I can say what the reason was, it is of an economic nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying it was your personal choice to leave the police?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: At my personal request I left on the 15th of February, 2005, that is to say at my personal request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in paragraphs 18 to 20 of your statement you tell us about the formation of local Albanian security groups in villages. How many of these were actually formed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that as I arrived in the territory of the SUP of Djakovica and since I knew certain persons of Albanian ethnicity who are my friends, I managed through them to deal with quite a few people who were involved in the local security. And thanks to the Catholic priest who was a priest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please just answer my question. How many of these village groups were actually formed?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: About 56 in Djakovica, 56 or 57. There must be a report, but let's not waste time now as I would leaf through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you mean the Djakovica town or do you mean the municipality?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Everything I'm saying, I'm saying at the level of the secretariat, regardless of whether it's Mitrovica or Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you have in front of you paragraph 42 of your statement where you say: "It was necessary to engage a large number of MUP members from Serbia," by which I mean -- I assume you mean outwith Kosovo, "in order to protect the population." First of all, what period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: The period of my stay in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this paragraph refers only to Kosovska Mitrovica. Do you mean it to also cover Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who were the large number of MUP members from Serbia that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who were the large number of MUP members from Serbia that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: These were regular policemen who were employed in the secretariats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And by that do you mean throughout the seven secretariats in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can speak only of the two where I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how many police officers were imported from across the Kosovo border into the two secretariats where you worked?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: They were not brought in. They applied when there were job vacancies that were publicised, and it is on the basis of these vacancy announcements that they were employed in the Djakovica and Mitrovica SUPs respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, paragraph 42 doesn't make any sense if that's what it's meant to mean. That's not what it says, Mr. Bogunovic. It says that because the MUP forces regularly in Kosovska Mitrovica were so heavily engaged in their work it was necessary to bring in reinforcements. That's how it reads. Are you saying that's wrong?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, fine, fine. I misspoke. This pertains to a group of policemen, or rather, the policemen who came from the PJPs, that's what it is about in paragraph 52, that came to the area of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's paragraph 42 I'm looking at, not 52. And if you make sure you've got the right page in front of you in your statement. In Kosovska Mitrovica what do you mean by a large number of MUP members? How many are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of the SUP of Kosovska Mitrovica, a detachment was engaged, a B variant detachment at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many men?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Between 400 and 600 men depending on what the personnel level is when they arrive in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you tell me where they came from, which PJP group they were?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the area of the SUP of Djakovica it was the Novi Sad Detachment, and in Kosovska Mitrovica it was the Uzice Detachment, one was the 8th and the other one was the 35th. Please don't take my word for it, for the numbers, that is, I'm not a PJP member so I may be making a mistake in terms of the numbers. But some came from the area of Vojvodina and others came from the area of metropolitan Uzice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when you say 4 to 600 men a detachment, you mean 4 to 600 men in Djakovica and 4 to 600 men in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA BOGUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have to break there now because we've reached the end of our time for today. I have a few more questions to ask you which I shall complete tomorrow. Mr. Lukic, can you give me an estimate of how long your re-examination might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we will resume the hearing tomorrow afternoon, Mr. Bogunovic. Meanwhile, it's vital that you have no communication with anyone, anyone at all, about any aspect of the evidence in this case, and that means evidence given or evidence yet to come in the case, and you should return here ready to continue your evidence at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Now would you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will act in accordance with your order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of April, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
